en: When the world was spacious,
When my sultan was alive,
Why did I not die then?
When my marten-fur cap, adorned in pairs,
Swayed upon my head,
When, ruling all the world,
My precious lord was alive,
When I lived in sheer delight,
Why did I not die then?
When at my threshold Zulpukor
Hung there on display,
When I, a woman, raised my head as a banner,
Made the people my banner,
And governed them,
Why did I not die then?
When all who had been scattered
I was gathering together,
When all that had been severed
I was joining once again,
Why did I not die just then?
When my companion lord was alive,
I raised a harrier into a hunting bird;
I gathered scattered groups into a people.
I reared a stray bird into a hunting bird;
I made a people of the wanderers.
The stray bird found a mountain to escape to;
When the ocean's eyes closed in death,
The wanderers became my enemies.
The harrier found a mountain to fly to;
After the leopard's eyes closed in death,
Those gathered groups became my enemies.
My treasury was left abandoned,
Gold and silver mingled there.
God, please hear my plea:
The son left in my care is young!
When the leopard's eyes closed in death,
O God, you plunged my mind into misery.
Let me take him as my companion,
My child left behind by my blood-shedding hero,
As I stand weeping in the wilds,
Let them not seize my head and press me down,
Nor bring more humiliation upon me,
Nor snatch my orphan from my hands.
Digging pit upon pit for me,
Let those accursed ones not boil up
My bitterest misfortune.
From the hoof the winged steed left behind,
Shall I truly be parted—
From the little one, my matchless treasure?
I have no strength to gird myself,
No people to give me support,
No renowned blood-shedding lion.
Without abandoning myself to pointless anguish,
By sitting wailing in the wilds,
What desire could I fulfill?
Now that the world has closed upon me,
Let me go to my birth family, Temir Khan!
Gathering courage and hurrying,
The gray pouch-belt fallen from heaven
She fastened at her waist.
Taking the battle-axe in hand,
Calling out, 'My generous one!'
Walking briskly, without lingering,
She headed toward the hills.
Water streamed from her nose;
From her dear eyes flowed tears mingled with blood.
That ill-intentioned Karymbai,
Excitedly driving his calf,
Having plunged the fierce woman into torment,
Hurried toward his village,
Driving his calf before him.
To everyone he met
Karymbai kept saying:
'She never gave up her greed,
The countless riches Manas left—
Those countless riches did not satisfy her.
She never gave up her greed.
My calf, suckled by a cow not bearing again,
She seized upon the slope,
To slaughter it secretly,
To gorge herself on its meat.
That bitch of a woman, Kanykei,
Had stolen my calf!
I knocked the arrogance right out of her,
That fierce bitch of a woman—
I lashed her side wide open.
I gave her a dream she will never forget,
Did a deed that will never leave her heart.
I brought her level with the black earth,
Made her tears a flood.
I relieved her itching place;
I opened her eyes, small as dough pellets!'
Saying this, Karymbai
Joined his company, boasting.
Walking bent toward the hills,
Your sister-in-law's tears flowed.
The broad pastures stretching in rows—
She wept at the sight of their land.
The dear Kyrgyz people blessed by Khizyr—
She wept at the sight of her people.
The hill where they climbed to keep watch—
She wept at the sight of its ridge.
The familiar Talas and Keng-Kol—
She wept at the sight of their banks.
In former days, when he was king,
Where Manas had sat—
She wept at the sight of his throne.
The royal sultan Bakai—
She wept at the sight of his garden.
The former games and days of happiness—
She wept, recalling those times.
'In sorrow, on this dark day,
What shall I do, staying here?
Let me set out sooner on the road
And wander away to Bukhara.
It is Allah's command;
Now let me reach my mother.'
Into Üyrülmö's desert hills
Your sister-in-law turned and went.
The rolling, pale, sunless slope—
She walked along its lower side.
Across its rough, mottled, sunless slope
Your sister-in-law walked, sobbing.
Where Manas's sheep had grazed,
At the white salt lick in the hills,
She lay beside the white salt lick.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei,
Resting on her elbow, slept;
She took a peaceful little nap.
As her eyes fell shut in sleep,
A brown two-year-old wether left by Manas,
A wether suckled by two mothers,
Came running up to her.
For those still living, fresh fish may come!
Your mother rejoiced greatly,
Starting awake from sleep.
To God, whose command is mighty,
She offered supplication now.
The shamefaced woman who had tired before
Reached out and stretched her hand.
It was truly the Creator's gift:
When your sister-in-law reached out,
Its shank came into her hand.
Invoking Baabedin's blessing,
Vowing a sheep to Koroshon,
Her dangling hair beads
She fitted about her neck.
To her beloved Manas, the morning star,
She prayed, invoking his spirit.
Taking the inner, shorter path,
Toward her orphan Kanykei went,
Leading the brown wether.
In a cave of Kaiyp-Kyr,
Chyiyrdy lay in hiding,
Showing her destitution.
As Kanykei drew near,
The little one left by the blood-shedder,
The infant still of cradle age,
She cheered and made to laugh;
Chyiyrdy brought him out.
A river like a shining lake,
The venerable, pure old lady,
The old woman of eighty years,
That blood-shedding leopard Manas—
She was the holy woman who bore him.
Among sons she bore a lion;
Among daughters she bore a hero.
The son she bore, Khan Manas,
Became khan of an established people.
The daughter she bore, Kardygach,
Became renowned among the Chinese.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei—
The banner in her hand,
From her king, Lord Manas,
Which eighty-year-old Chyiyrdy
Held as the gift he left—
Each time she looked, her hunger was sated.
He had no companion but his mother,
No strength to gird himself.
The old lady made him her support;
She had no other people besides him.
Before the old woman,
She turned her face toward the Truth.
The lawful livestock left by Manas—
Before the old lady
She offered the wether as a gift.
The two ladies dipped their hands in water,
Performing ablution of their hands;
They dipped their feet in water,
Performing ablution of their feet.
To slaughter the brown wether
The two ladies made ready.
In former days, your dear sister-in-law Kanykei,
When she was the fairest of women,
The youngest of twelve daughters,
A servant beloved of God,
In the gardens of great Bukhara,
When she played there,
Still a little girl herself,
Her hair not yet long enough to braid,
Had saddled her white winged steed.
The glorious, sacred Quran
She had read as a girl.
The surah called Tappat
She read with astonishing speed;
The Quran's Kulkuldabat
She recited fittingly from memory.
Spreading her palms, hastening,
To Manas, gone to the other world,
To his spirit, as two meals' worth,
She dedicated the brown wether.
The mottled-necked Ak Tinte
She drew out of its sheath.
Your precious sister-in-law Kanykei,
Her eyes shining like a camel calf's,
One part of the white blade's handle
She had her orphan Semetey hold.
As a ritual, the brown wether—
She slaughtered the brown wether now.
Committing its soul to Allah,
Your sister-in-law Kanykei
Cut off its head.
When all their wealth was scattered,
Your mountainlike mother Chyiyrdy,
The infant still of cradle age
Clasped against her breast,
Running toward the hills,
Despairing of her precious life,
When she fled this way,
Your lion mother Chyiyrdy
A merciless calamity
Had brought upon them indeed!
'If anything appears, I shall slaughter it,
And give my orphan one full meal,' she had said.
The little cauldron left by Manas
Your mother had brought along!
The stand and stones for the hearth
She set out ready now.
Dry firewood giving off no smoke—
Your exhausted sister-in-law Kanykei
Gathered it on the plain.
Beseeching her Allah,
All the brown wether's meat
She put in, leaving nothing out.
Your capable mother Kanykei,
Cooking it in no time,
Brought it to a vigorous boil.
The hind shank and meat of the hip,
The finest of all the joints,
She gave to her mother Chyiyrdy.
Its thick fat tail, big as a cauldron,
She gave to Semetey.
The neck meat with its bones
Quickly stirred his appetite.
He was still an infant of cradle age,
Just six months old.
